- I think we've mentioned
a few themes here
around the integration, right?

You have things like
electromagnetic analysis

and just pure design
suites being brought in
alongside CAE suites.
But what do you think is the next round
of cross-disciplinary integration?
- Looking at where we are today,

just getting all these
workflows sorted out
is a challenge in its own right.

I do see AI having impact
in areas, you know,

like certainly in CAE there
has to be a lot of testing
and benchmarking and so on.
I could see AI playing a big place there.
In terms of the coding,
I think it will change in the CAE space.
I assume it'll be the, the same in EDA,

so that, you know, the
developers will be focusing
on the high value stuff
and the more, you know, churny stuff,

that can be done with
artificial intelligence.

(bright music)
- Hello, everyone, and welcome
to the "Altium OnTrack Podcast."
I'm your host, Zach Peterson.
Today we're talking with Keith Hanna,

independent consultant
for the CAE PLM industry.
If you have been paying attention

to what's been going
on in the EDA industry,
you're probably aware that there have been
some very high profile acquisitions,

including the acquisition
of Altium by Renesas.

I thought Keith would be
a very interesting person

to talk to about this,
given his experience

in the industry and across
a variety of fields.

Keith, thank you so much
for being here today.
- Thank you.
Thank you for inviting me.

- So before we get started
talking about some of the stuff
that's been going on in the EDA industry
and engineering software in general,

do me a favor, tell us
about your background

and how you got involved
in your current field.

- Okay, well, I'm actually
a chemical engineer
by background.
I did a PhD in chemical engineering,

though my first degree
was actually in mining.

So I've come a long way
into engineering software,

but the thread through it
all has been during my PhD,
I started to write some code in the 1980s

to solve the equations for
fluid flow and heat transfer.

And from that, I got a
job where I got exposed

to a software, a very early
piece of software called Fluent,

which was a CFD code,
computational fluid dynamics.

And I stayed in that
industry for about 18 years
as it grew from very small

to maybe a quarter of a
million a year in 2006
where it got acquired by Ansys.
And I stayed and got involved in Ansys
for three years in multiphysics.
And then I moved into
where it was still mechanical analysis,

but it was a company
called Mentor Graphics,
as some of your listeners will know about,

which is one of the big three
EDA companies back in the day
and had a really interesting experience
and exposed me to the EDA industry,

given my background was mainly
CAD, mechanical analysis,
a bit of architectural work as well.

And then stayed with Mentor
until it was acquired
by Siemens in 2017, I think it was.
And then in 2018, I left and went to work
for another manufacturing company
that had some interest in electronics,
and that was a company called Hexagon

who had acquired a very old
CAE company called MSC Software

and they brought me in as
vice president of marketing
to help turn around the marketing there.

And then about two years
ago, I left Hexagon
to become an independent consultant,

mainly working with small and
medium sized CAE companies

and, laterally, I actually
have also partnered up

with a company called Cambashi
in Cambridge here in the UK

that does market
analysis, market research,

and CAE PLM industry,
not a lot in the EDA,
but I do put out blogs.

And recently I put out
a blog that Zach saw

on my opinions on the
EDA industry clashing
with the CAE industry
because I think it is a game changer
for both industries actually.

And there a variety of reasons
behind it, in my opinion.
- So before we go further,
you've mentioned CAE a couple of times.
For any listeners that aren't aware,

could you please just
give us a brief overview
of what CAE software is?

- Well, CAE or mechanical
computer-aided engineering
is a series of disciplines.

The one that I started off
with was fluid dynamics.

In terms of physics, we've
known about the equations

of fluid flow, heat transfer,
transfer of materials
for the last 150 years,

but it was only with the
advent of digital computers
in the 70s that we started to be able
to solve these equations simultaneously

and in real space and time
in a way that was useful
for predicting mechanical effects.
So that was fluid dynamics.

It kind of came out of
Imperial College here in the UK
in the 1960s and 70s, but prior to that,

there was some work done
on structural analysis,

came a lot out of the
moonshots of the 60s actually

because we'll need to simulate
the structural effects,

structural stresses and
strains and cracking and so on,

and that's been going
for about 50, 60 years.

And then the other big
areas are electromagnetics,
which obviously dovetails very nicely.

Well, in fact, all these areas
dovetailed nicely with EDA.
It's just that historically,

EDA industry grew separately
from the CAE industry,
from the CAD industry,
and computer or manufacturing as well.

And of course, now with so
much electronics embedded
in mechanical products,
that they're becoming intertwined
and seamless in many respects.

- So obviously you have a
lot of experience working
in these areas of software,
and you've identified one evolution,

which is, I think, probably
part of a broader trend

or a broader theme across
engineering disciplines
or engineering software.
What can you tell us about that

and what evolutions have
you observed over time?

- Well, as I said, what
I think I've observed

is I've obviously come
from mechanical background,

you know, did a bit of
electrical engineering
at college and very little electronics.
And obviously, you know, you go into work,
and I worked in the real world
before I got into software,

and you're solving mechanical
problems essentially.

But I've noticed maybe
over the last 25 years,
even if you think of our automobiles,

you know, how much electronics
there is in them today,

essentially, when you go
to buy your latest SUV,

you're buying electronics
box on wheels, basically.
The mechanical side is still there,

but it's all being driven
by CPUs and control boxes

and, you know, LED lights
and a host of things.

And in fact, BMW, reckon,
maybe half the value
of their car is the electronics,

and a lot of the profitability
is in the electronics.
So electronics has become embedded

in a lot of consumer
products, mechanical products

in particular in the auto
industry, aero industry,

but consumer electronics in
it generally has exploded,
I would say, during my career,

and that has essentially
meant that if you want
to design a mechanical product,

you have to take into account
electronics and vice versa.
The two are unavoidable.

And usually, you find,
you know, as electronics,

you know, when I was
working in Mentor Graphics,
they were primarily quite strong on PCBs.

And obviously PCBs are
in every control unit,

but as they become more
denser in electronics

and integrated circuits and
all sorts of power electronics
has come in now as well,

it starts to have strong
mechanical effects like thermal.

Thermal is the biggest source
of failure for electronics.

And obviously if an
electronic component fails,
the whole of the mechanical product fails.
So being able to simulate thermal effects,

stresses, and cracking,
vibrations, dust, and humidity

can also, you know, cause
failure of electronics.

So, all of these need to
be simulated more and more

we're discovering in all of
the major industry sectors.
And obviously, EDA has come out
of the semiconductor industry,

but I kind of view
electronics as both a vertical
and a horizontal in an industrial sense.
And by that I mean it's a vertical
in terms of semiconductor manufacturing,
but electronics appears in automotive,
in aerospace, in consumer products.

Pretty much every other
industry sector has electronics.
So it transcends the horizontal,
and that's why I think EDA has grown
so much over the last 10, 20 years.
And what is probably most interesting,
it's come in and taken over the CAE

or is starting to stake
over the CAE market.

And increasingly, PLM,
product lifecycle management,
is colliding into EDA,
and, you know, Cambashi, reckon,

EDA is maybe about $15 billion
a year including Altium.

PLM, which includes CAE,
is about 30 billion.
CAE is about eight billion.
So those are sort of numbers.
They're all kind of growing
at this 10% year on year organic growth,
but it's still nowhere near saturated,
and there's still a huge opportunity
and head room for growth
as I'm sure folks at Altium know that.
- So what I'm really hearing here
is kind of a fusion across disciplines,
and I bring this up because if you look

at some of the fusion or
integration in the recent past,

particularly between,
you know, PCB and MCAD,
it has a lot to do with like placement,
you know, placement route.

It has a lot to do with
fitting in an enclosure,
which are obviously really important

because they're such huge
drivers of the user experience
and the usability of a product.

So I don't mean to, you know,
minimalize that or anything,

but it, it seems to me that
there's been an inability

to access some of these
higher level important things

that you mentioned, things
like thermal simulation,
things like CFD, especially I think,
for power products that use airflow
for cooling and stuff like that.

It's not only is the
software more specialized,

but the direct integrations
just haven't been there
really until recently.
Would you agree?

- Yeah, well, actually,
the company Mentor Graphics
that they acquired that I worked with

for about eight, 10 years,
a company called Flomerics,

they tried to span the two
sides of the chasm as it were,
and obviously, Mentor subsequently
became quite proficient at it,
but it is super difficult
because the skillset are very different
in the EDA than they are in mechanical.
And the timeframes are different as well.

Obviously for any consumer
product, you want to be able

to virtually test it
as quickly as possible.

And in the early design, you
wanna do as much simulation
before you commit to a prototype,

and obviously, you ideally
wanna get it right first time.
And I've designed out all potential flaws.
And as I said, one of the things

that I've observed in
certainly my interactions
with the EDA industry is the language
is completely different in electronics
and compared to mechanical.

So when I first appeared at
Mentor Graphics in Portland,
everybody's talking systems,
and in my brain, I'm thinking systems

in terms of mechanical
systems or fluid systems,

whereas in electronics has a
very, very different meaning.
And so, there's always this concern

that, yes, an electronic PCB
or an IC could be designed,

and then it was thrown over
a wall to the mechanical guys
and then thrown back again.
And you would get this sort of ping pong
that was going on.
And ideally, you want it to be iterative

and they're both speaking
the same language,

not in a actual sense,
but in a figurative sense.
And actually the key thing
is what is now called the digital thread.
It's we generate shared loads of data.
You know, in simulation,
you can get terabytes of data very easily,
particularly in the mechanical space.

And then how do you use that
data in a very intelligent way,
both from the electronic design space
and then the mechanical analysis space,
but also the CAD space.

And then ultimately, actually
all electronic products
have to be manufactured,

and you actually have other
software involved as well

like embedded software,
which also has to be designed
and applied to these products.
And then in manufacturing,
you have MES software, ERP software.
There's this huge thread of simulations

and data all the way
through a modern product,
and that's just to have it manufactured.

And then obviously during
use, it deteriorates,
it may fail, it may be recalled.

There may be all sorts of
issues that weren't anticipated.
And then ultimately,

in, you know, the modern
sustainable world,
we wanna recycle all this stuff.

So somehow getting all that
together is super difficult.

And do I think any company's
doing it all today?
No, not really.

You get ones that are good
at one part of the spectrum
and one's good at the other.

The only one that I've seen
is Siemens when I was there,
and that was quite an interesting one

because they were essentially
a mechanical company,
you know, 200 years of history,
got into CAD maybe 15 years ago,
then got into computer-aided engineering
and then acquired Mentor Graphics.
I think Mentor Graphics

was the first significant
EDA PLM interaction
in terms of a big acquisition.

And today, you know, they're
stitching all this together,

and they have, you know,
layers of other software
underneath for data management.

And then obviously, you know,
I'm not even talking about AI.
You know, that's coming in,

and that's gonna impact
the whole of the industry
in ways still to be determined.
- Yeah, it wouldn't be an Altium podcast
if we didn't mention AI.
Now, (chuckles) you mentioned acquisition-
- Well, I would say actually

from my perspective in
the PLM CAE industry,
the acronym or the word AI is used.
I'm not sure it's real AI at the moment.

I think there's still a lot
of machine learning going on,

which, you know, I've seen
work and is very effective.
True AI really depends on good algorithms

and enough data to train
the algorithms well.

I can't speak, you know,
much for the EDA industry,

but I do know in the computer-aided
engineering industry,
you can predict the wrong answer as much

as the right answer if you
miss out certain physics
or you make assumptions and so on.

So, you know, AI could just
accelerate that failure,

if you see what I mean,
if it's applied wrongly.
- So getting back to acquisition.

Excuse me, getting back to
acquisitions for just a moment,
M&A is not a new thing in our industry,

whether it's CAE or PCB
or EDA or whatever, right?
M&A has been going on for a long time.
I think one of the earlier M&A activities
within the last five years, obviously,
you know, Siemens acquiring Mentor.
I think that raised a lot of eyebrows.

But you know, it seems to
have culminated in 2024
where we've had a pretty huge year
in terms of M&A activity
in a lot of high profile acquisitions,

particularly of names that
I think people thought
were always gonna be independent.
So, what makes all this activity different
from prior rounds of M&A?
Is it just deal sizes?

Is it the peculiarity of
cross cross-discipline M&A?

You know, I mean, with
Renesas acquiring Altium,

it's a semiconductor manufacturer
acquiring a PCB company.

I think that makes people
scratch their heads a little bit.

What do you see as being
different this round of M&A
compared to prior rounds?
- That's a good question.

I would say the
electrification of everything,
which goes back to my earlier point
on, you know, when I buy a mobile phone,
I'm buying a mini computer,
which, you know, is more powerful
than what I used to have on my desktop
probably 10, 20 years ago.
So the electrification of everything,

or electronicification,
if that's the right word,
of everything has a huge impact.
If I look at it purely from the CAE side,
if I look at a company like Ansys,

the big shock was Ansys
being acquired by Synopsys,
you know, 'cause they're not far
off the same size actually.

There's maybe only a few
billion dollars a year
between them in terms of revenues.

Ansys itself was notorious
in the CAE PLM space,

was just acquiring companies
over the last 20 years,
including the one that I started off in
and very good at taking them
and accelerating the revenue growth
from the companies they acquired.

So they became essentially
a multiphysics company.
Yes, they acquired Apache
and got a bit into the electronic space,
but not in terms of pure EDA.

And then of course,
obviously you've Synopsys
who maybe had a bit of optical simulation,
but not a lot of other pure CAE play.

So that is the big play
that is most interesting.

And it'll be fascinating
to see how it plays out,

to be honest, because you have
two very different cultures.
You know, will Synopsys come in,
put their own people on board?

Will they leave Ansys, you
know, as a revenue generator?

Will they start to integrate
products a bit more?
We simply don't know.

You know, the potential
there is to add value,

but like as with all
acquisitions, you know,
at least half of them can fail
according to shareholder value.
So, it's to be determined.
I think Siemens have done pretty well

with Mentor Graphics
from what I understand.

And obviously, they've just
announced this big acquisition

for Altair, which is
another mainly CAE company.
Yes, they have some electromagnetics,
which I think Siemens really wanted.
And so that will be more than add-on
I would say it Siemens.
What is interesting is the multipliers.

You know, 18x, 16x, wow,
those are big numbers.
So someone's expecting huge growth there.
I think 10, 15 years ago in CAE,
the multipliers were maybe 6x, 8x.

So now that we're up at
twice that, maybe plus,
that is really fascinating,
and, you know, yeah you could say Synopsys

are betting the farm on
this one, aren't they?

- (chuckles) Yeah, that's
what it seems like.
The multipliers, I think they were
a bit eyebrow raising too,

because like you said,
they used to be smaller.
But I wonder if part of that

is just because if you
look, you know, broader

within the market for
publicly traded securities,
the multipliers are already higher
because growth is so good.
Everybody's doing so well.
They just had to pay more.
They had to make the offer rich.
- And from a CAE perspective,

there aren't that many of
these independents left.

You know, in the last
year, Altair has gone.
ESI has been acquired by Keysight,
which is kind of electronics company.
Very interesting acquisition there.
So, basically if an electronics company
wants some mechanical analysis,
you know, better start looking around

'cause there aren't
that many big ones left.
I can only think of two or three

that are, you know, still
potentially available
and vice versa.

So I think this may be
a need in the EDA side.
And also it's interesting
to see how the PLM will respond to this.
'cause the PLM world is, is very much,
in my opinion, driven by geometry.

It's came out of the mechanical
CAD, the CAD industry.

And then CAD is used in
manufacturing and so on.

And obviously, EDA has come
from a different direction.
So how these two will interface
will be really fascinating, in my opinion.
- So do you think that on balance,

this is all going to be a
good thing for engineers?
Now I ask this because whenever something
like this comes up,
existing user base for these products,
I think many of them complain.
Maybe complain is not the right word,

but they express a lot
of fear that the tool
that they love is going to change so much
or the price is gonna go so high
that it's no longer accessible to them.
And I don't want to downplay that.
You know, I do wanna be cognizant of that,

but given enough time
and given enough effort
by the companies involved in these deals,

do you think it's going to
be on balance a good thing
for the existing users and for new users?
- Well, there's always the argument,

are you, you know, reducing
the field, you know?

Your less choice usually
means more of monopoly.

Prices can go up, you
know, yada yada, yada.
The other side of the equation
is, you know, if I look at Siemens again,
they acquired Mentor Graphics,

they've invested a lot in CAD
underneath the EDA products,
and I see huge improvements there

compared to if they hadn't
acquired Mentor Graphics.
So it wouldn't have been as far forward
with the products there.

And also you get access to
other products in the suite
that Mentor Graphics or Siemens offer.

And I would expect the same
with Synopsys and Ansys
and similarly with Cadence and BETA CAE.

To be honest, the one
I still struggle with
is Altium and Renesas.
Yes, I can see it at one level
from a pure electronics play,

but I'm not sure on the
wider PLM MCAE market
if it has that much impact.

- I think we've mentioned
a few themes here
around the integration, right?

You have things like
electromagnetic analysis

and just pure design
suites being brought in
alongside CAE suites.
But what do you think is the next round
of cross-disciplinary integration?
I have an idea that I can speculate on,
really maybe two ideas, right?
One of them could be something

where I guess you bring
embedded software developers
back into the fold of electronics design
because currently, everything they do
is totally isolated, right?
None of that stuff talks to each other.

The closest they get to talking
to each other is on GitHub.

And then probably the other
one is something to do with AI.
- Looking at where we are today,

just getting all these
workflows sorted out
is a challenge in its own right.

I do see AI having impact
in areas, you know,
like certainly in CAE there has to be

a lot of testing and
benchmarking and so on.
I can see AI playing a big place there.
In terms of the coding,
I think it will change in the CAE space.
I assume it'll be the same in EDA

so that, you know, the
developers will be focusing
on the high value stuff
and the more, you know, churny stuff,

that can be done with
artificial intelligence.

I think just doing what
we're doing better and faster

is a significant step
forward if I can say that.
And don't forget, we've also got,
at least in the PLM CAE,
certainly in the computer-aid engineering,
it's terribly number crunching.
You know, it literally is rocket science.
Literally, you know, when I first did

a Formula 1 simulation of
a complete car in 1996,
it took six months to do it.

You know, today, they're may
be doing it in 10 minutes,

but they really want
everything in real time
as quickly as possible,

which in EDA is more,
you know, acceptable,

but in the mechanical space,
we're still behind there.
And you know, with what Nvidia are doing
with their processors and cloud computing,

I think is also gonna ha
have a significant play.
And actually cloud still hasn't really...
I don't know what it's like with Altium,

maybe you can comment, but
in the mechanical space,
it's more used as an auxiliary
rather than a pay per use model.
That still hasn't really come to pass

because a lot of the
mechanical simulation tools
are still very hard use.
You don't quite know exactly what you need
when you start a simulation.

So having a general purpose
code can make a lot of sense,
but it is very intensive.
So, I think all of those things
plus data management and data mining...
You know, someone once told me

there are millions, probably
billions of simulations

are done each year, but
very little of the data

is used intelligently to
help subsequent simulations
'cause it's all kept proprietary
within the customer base.
Now, I think that's a huge opportunity

that still hasn't been mined
in the PLM field at least.

- Yeah, I you brought up cloud,
which I think is interesting

because, you know, obviously
Altium is, you know, trying

to lead in the cloud thanks
to the Altium 365 platform.

I think usually when
people hear cloud and EDA,

they think, oh, you're putting
my PCB design tool online

or you're putting, you know,
my packaging design tool
or whatever online or you're putting
my simulator online, right?
I think those are the obvious ones.
It doesn't always work out

because, you know, online
requires a lot of bandwidth
to even do some of those activities.

But there are probably
opportunities with cloud

that no one in the EDA
space has even thought of,
and you kind of hinted at one,
which is like infrastructure.
- I think maybe the mechanical world

is ahead of the EDA world
in terms of using cloud

because it maybe had to
because it wants this speed up,

and that's possibly
where EDA will learn more
from the mechanical side than vice versa.

Yeah, the problem is sometimes
you give them one hand,
you take away with another.

Yes, it's great, we've
got so many data centers,

but what is it, data
centers now are, what, 8%
of world emissions of CO2,

and, you know, we're not
building them fast enough
and so on.
So, maybe there is an argument

for a lot of these
engineering simulation tools

to be more efficient
than what they are today,
better architected, better designed
'cause a lot of them are like a house

that's had a wing built
here and another wing
and then another floor put on top.
You know, they're not optimal in many ways

for the modern, you know,
computer code as it were.
- Yeah, I think that makes a lot of sense.
So would you be willing to speculate
what might be some of the next names
to be acquired by the bigger players?

And maybe if you can't
mention specific names, maybe-

- Oh, I can mention
names because it's not...

I can observe the market
like anyone else can.
If I look at it from a PLM perspective,
the company that seems to, you know, need

to move now is Dassault,
which is one of the big three,
or big four or five PLM companies
who doesn't have much in the EDA space.
So are they out looking?
You know, is Zuken free?
Who knows?
You know, Zuken is one
of the last big independents, isn't it?
I think Dassault probably still needs
some fluid dynamics capability,
and there are some independents there
they might be interested in.

PTC, does Cadence want to
get into CAD, you know?

Like is there a nice marriage
made in heaven there?
You could look at it that way.
And then Autodesk, they're there.
What's happening with them?
Are they gonna get into EDA in some way
because I don't think you can afford
to be off this bandwagon.

The bandwagon has started,
you know, with Siemens
and Mentor and now Synopsys and Cadence.

How's everybody else
gonna respond to this?

And obviously Altium, you
know, like Altium, as I say,

that was a bit of a left
field one with Renesas, but...
- Yeah, it's interesting

because it feels like all
of this is coming at a time
after we had a semiconductor shock
due to COVID and due to demand spikes,

and all of a sudden, there
is worldwide investment
in that production capacity.

So now there's renewed
focus on electronics.
And then it suddenly seems like,

oh, there's all this really
great software out there
that's making a lot of money,
and we see the market growth.

Now all of a sudden, it
seems like the right time
to invest in these companies.
- I think there's another factor going on,

and I'll probably comment
on it sometime next year,
and, you know, it's a sad factor.
It's geopolitics.
Let's be honest.

You know, even my daughter
came home from school

and said, "Is it gonna be
a World War III, Daddy?"
Wow, you know, this is from a 12-year-old.
And of course, I say, "I hope not,"
but you know, in my career, you know,

I've been through the Cold
War when I was younger,

then, you know, the
fall of the Berlin Wall,
and then everybody was friends
and we were going globalization full guns,
and now, we've got this situation

where there's several,
you know, very nasty wars
going on in the world.
And of course, don't forget,
all of this technology is dual use.
And I think part of the impetus,

the growth in this is,
you know, the demand
for defense, the demand for military.
And look at you guys in the US.

You know, concern over PCB,
you know, in Taiwan and so on.
So there are multiple factors going on
in the background that didn't exist,
or at least we weren't concerned about it
10, 15 years ago, I'd say.
- That's a really good point.
I had not even thought of,

you know, geopolitics
playing a role in this,

but I think that probably
looms in the background,
